Phil 4:6-7.ctx: Paul writes to the church in Philippi while imprisoned; just before this he urges them to rejoice in the Lord and let their gentleness be known to all, because “the Lord is at hand” (vv. 4–5).
Phil 4:6-7.meaning: When worries come, bring everything to God specifically and with thanksgiving; what God promises is a peace that guards the heart, not necessarily an immediate change in circumstances.
Phil 4:6-7.caution: “In nothing be anxious” is an invitation to hand our worries to God, not a rebuke for feeling anxious.

Matt 6:31-34.ctx: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus teaches his disciples not to worry about food and clothing, pointing to the birds of the sky and the lilies of the field (vv. 25–30).
Matt 6:31-34.meaning: The Father knows what we need; the disciple’s priority is to seek first God’s Kingdom and righteousness, and to let each day’s trouble be enough for that day.
Matt 6:31-34.caution: This doesn’t mean we shouldn’t work or plan; it means not being ruled by worry.

1Pet 5:6-7.ctx: Peter writes to scattered believers who are suffering; just before this he urges elders and younger people alike to clothe themselves with humility (vv. 1–5).
1Pet 5:6-7.meaning: Humble yourselves under God’s mighty hand and cast all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

Isa 41:10.ctx: God speaks through the prophet to exiled Israel, whose future is uncertain; the nations are panicking and making idols for security (vv. 5–7), but God reminds Israel that it is his chosen servant, not rejected (vv. 8–9).
Isa 41:10.meaning: The covenant God himself is present to strengthen, help, and uphold his people.
Isa 41:10.caution: These words were first spoken to Israel; what we can apply is God’s faithfulness to be with those who are his, not a guarantee that things will turn out the way we expect.

Ps 56:3-4.ctx: A psalm David wrote while fleeing Saul, when the Philistines seized him in Gath (see the title and 1 Samuel 21).
Ps 56:3-4.meaning: In times of fear, choose to trust God, and let God’s word be the reason for praise.
Ps 56:3-4.caution: The text admits there are times of fear; faith is not pretending not to be afraid.

Ps 27:1.ctx: A psalm of trust David wrote while surrounded by enemies; the second half also contains earnest pleading (vv. 7–12).
Ps 27:1.meaning: The Lord is light, salvation, and the stronghold of life, so we need not be ruled by people or circumstances.

Ps 34:18.ctx: A psalm of thanksgiving David wrote after pretending to be insane before Abimelech (Achish king of Gath) and escaping (see the title).
Ps 34:18.meaning: God does not stay far from the brokenhearted; he draws near to them and saves those who are crushed in spirit.

1Thess 4:13-14.ctx: The believers in Thessalonica were worried about what would happen to fellow believers who had died when the Lord returns; Paul answers their question.
1Thess 4:13-14.meaning: Believers can grieve, but not like those who have no hope; because Jesus died and rose again, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.
1Thess 4:13-14.caution: The text does not say “don’t grieve.” This promise is spoken about those who died in the Lord; if the faith of the person who died is unclear, use it gently and don’t jump to conclusions.

Rev 21:3-4.ctx: John sees a vision of the new heaven and new earth and the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven, the final hope of the whole Bible.
Rev 21:3-4.meaning: God will dwell with his people and wipe away every tear himself; there will be no more death, mourning, crying, or pain.
Rev 21:3-4.caution: This is a future hope; it does not deny the tears of the present.

Ps 73:26.ctx: Asaph had nearly slipped because the wicked prospered while he suffered (vv. 2–3), until he went into God’s sanctuary and understood (v. 17).
Ps 73:26.meaning: Even when body and heart fail, God is still the strength of the heart and our portion forever.

2Cor 4:16-18.ctx: Paul describes being pressed on every side and suffering in his body as he serves (vv. 7–12), then explains why he does not lose heart.
2Cor 4:16-18.meaning: Though the outer person is decaying, the inner person is renewed day by day; compared with the glory to come, present troubles are light and momentary.
2Cor 4:16-18.caution: “Light and momentary” is Paul’s comparison from the perspective of eternity, not a call to dismiss the pain someone is going through.

2Cor 12:9-10.ctx: Paul had a “thorn in the flesh”; three times he begged the Lord to remove it, and the Lord did not remove it as he asked (vv. 7–8).
2Cor 12:9-10.meaning: God’s grace is sufficient, and his power is made perfect in human weakness.
2Cor 12:9-10.caution: This passage shows that prayer does not always end in healing; it must not be used to suggest that an illness remains because of too little faith.

Matt 11:28-30.ctx: After rebuking the cities that would not repent, Jesus thanks the Father (vv. 20–27) and then extends this invitation to everyone.
Matt 11:28-30.meaning: All who labor and are heavily burdened can come to Jesus and find rest, learning from him and taking his easy yoke.
Matt 11:28-30.caution: A “yoke” still means following and learning; rest does not mean having no responsibilities at all.

Isa 40:28-31.ctx: The prophet speaks to exiled Israel, who complained, “My way is hidden from the Lord” (v. 27).
Isa 40:28-31.meaning: The God who created the heavens and the earth does not faint or grow weary; he gives strength to the weak, and those who wait for him will mount up with wings like eagles.

Ps 23:1-3.ctx: A psalm of trust David wrote from his experience as a shepherd, moving from green pastures to the valley of the shadow of death, and then to God’s table and house.
Ps 23:1-3.meaning: God is like a good shepherd who provides what is needed, gives rest, and restores the weary soul.

Heb 13:5-6.ctx: Practical exhortations near the end of Hebrews; just before this, the writer urges readers to be free from the love of money and content with what they have. “I will in no way leave you” quotes Deuteronomy 31:6.
Heb 13:5-6.meaning: God promises never to leave or forsake those who are his, so we can say with confidence, “The Lord is my helper.”

Ps 27:10.ctx: In the same psalm of trust, David asks God not to forsake him (v. 9).
Ps 27:10.meaning: Even if the people closest to us forsake us, the Lord will take us in.
Ps 27:10.caution: This verse uses “father and mother forsaking” to express the deepest loneliness; it does not say parents will surely forsake us.

Isa 49:15-16.ctx: Zion (exiled Israel) complains, “The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me” (v. 14), and God answers this way.
Isa 49:15-16.meaning: Even a mother may forget her nursing child, but God does not forget his people; he has engraved them on the palms of his hands.
Isa 49:15-16.caution: These words were first spoken to Zion; what we can apply is God’s faithfulness in not forgetting those who are his.

Ps 37:23-24.ctx: A wisdom psalm from David’s later years, urging people not to fret because of evildoers, but to trust the Lord and do good (vv. 1–8).
Ps 37:23-24.meaning: The Lord establishes the steps of the righteous; even if they stumble, they will not fall flat, because the Lord holds them up with his hand.
Ps 37:23-24.caution: It does not promise we will never stumble, but that God still upholds us when we do.

Mic 7:8.ctx: The prophet speaks to the enemy on behalf of Israel, which has sinned and is under discipline, admitting “I have sinned against the Lord” (v. 9) while still looking to God.
Mic 7:8.meaning: When we fall and sit in darkness, the Lord is still our light, and he will raise us up again.
Mic 7:8.caution: The original setting is hope after sin and discipline; when applying it to setbacks in general, the focus is “the Lord will be a light to me.”

Lam 3:21-26.ctx: A lament after the destruction of Jerusalem; the writer first pours out deep pain honestly (vv. 1–20), then turns to remembering God.
Lam 3:21-26.meaning: Because of the Lord’s loving kindness we are not consumed; his mercies are new every morning; he is good to those who wait for him and seek him.
Lam 3:21-26.caution: This hope appears after honest weeping; there is no need to rush past the sorrow.

1John 1:8-9.ctx: John writes to the church, pointing out that some claim to have no sin; he stresses walking in the light and confessing honestly (vv. 5–10).
1John 1:8-9.meaning: If we confess our sins, God is faithful and righteous to forgive us and cleanse us.

Ps 51:10-12.ctx: David’s psalm of repentance after his sin with Bathsheba was exposed by the prophet Nathan (see the title and 2 Samuel 12).
Ps 51:10-12.meaning: Repentance is not only asking for forgiveness, but also asking God to create a clean heart, renew a right spirit, and restore the joy of salvation.

Rom 8:1-2.ctx: In chapter 7 Paul describes the agony of struggling with sin; in chapter 8 he proclaims freedom in Christ.
Rom 8:1-2.meaning: There is no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus, because the law of the Spirit of life sets us free from the law of sin and death.
Rom 8:1-2.caution: No condemnation does not mean there is no need to repent; it means those who repent no longer have to live under condemnation.

Eph 4:31-32.ctx: Paul urges the Ephesian believers to put off the old self and put on the new (vv. 22–24), and to live it out in their speech and relationships.
Eph 4:31-32.meaning: Put away bitterness and anger; be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave us.
Eph 4:31-32.caution: Forgiveness does not mean denying the harm, nor does it require immediately restoring trust or staying in a dangerous relationship.

Col 3:12-14.ctx: Paul urges the Colossian believers that, since they have been raised with Christ, they should put on a new way of life (vv. 1–11).
Col 3:12-14.meaning: Bear with and forgive one another with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, and put on love, which binds everything together.

Matt 18:21-22.ctx: Peter asks Jesus how many times he should forgive his brother; Jesus then tells the parable of the unforgiving servant (vv. 23–35).
Matt 18:21-22.meaning: There is no upper limit on forgiveness, because we have first been forgiven an enormous debt by God.
Matt 18:21-22.caution: Forgiveness is a process; it does not require the person who was hurt to pretend immediately that nothing happened.

Jas 1:19-20.ctx: James encourages believers facing trials to be doers of the word, not hearers only (v. 22).
Jas 1:19-20.meaning: Be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger, because human anger does not produce the righteousness of God.

Eph 4:26-27.ctx: Part of the same “put on the new self” exhortation, about putting it into practice in speech and relationships.
Eph 4:26-27.meaning: Anger in itself is not necessarily sin, but don’t let the sun go down on your anger, and give no place to the devil.

Prov 15:1.ctx: One of Solomon’s wise sayings about speech.
Prov 15:1.meaning: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
Prov 15:1.caution: Proverbs are general principles of wisdom, not promises that the same thing will happen every time.

1Cor 13:4-7.ctx: The Corinthian church prized spiritual gifts but was divided; Paul writes this chapter on love between his discussions of gifts in chapters 12 and 14.
1Cor 13:4-7.meaning: Love is patient and kind and does not seek its own; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, and endures all things.
1Cor 13:4-7.caution: It was written to a church community and fits marriage and family well, but “endures all things” does not mean tolerating violence or abuse.

Eccl 4:9-12.ctx: The Teacher observes people who toil alone under the sun (vv. 7–8), then speaks of the value of companions.
Eccl 4:9-12.meaning: Two are better than one; when one falls, the other can lift them up; a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

Ps 127:1-2.ctx: A Song of Ascents by Solomon about home, city, and children as gifts from God.
Ps 127:1-2.meaning: Unless the Lord builds the house, its builders labor in vain; he gives sleep to his loved ones.

Ps 37:3-5.ctx: David urges people not to fret because of evildoers, for they will soon be cut down like grass (vv. 1–2).
Ps 37:3-5.meaning: Trust in the Lord and do good, delight yourself in the Lord, commit your way to him, and he will act.
Ps 37:3-5.caution: “The desires of your heart” is said on the basis of delighting in the Lord; it is not a guarantee of getting whatever we want.

Phil 4:11-13.ctx: Paul thanks the Philippian church for their gift and explains that in prison he has learned to be content (vv. 10–18).
Phil 4:11-13.meaning: Whether well fed or hungry, in plenty or in need, he has learned contentment; through him who strengthens him, he can face all things.
Phil 4:11-13.caution: Verse 13 is often taken to mean “with the Lord I’ll succeed at anything,” but its meaning is being content in both plenty and need.

Col 3:23-24.ctx: Paul addresses believers who were servants at the time (v. 22), reminding them that their work is done for the Lord.
Col 3:23-24.meaning: Whatever you do, work from the heart, as for the Lord, because the true reward comes from the Lord.
Col 3:23-24.caution: This was first said to servants of that time; what we can apply is our attitude to work, not that we should silently endure unjust treatment.

Prov 3:5-6.ctx: Solomon, speaking as a father, urges his son to hold on to wisdom and God’s instruction.
Prov 3:5-6.meaning: Trust in the Lord with all your heart, don’t lean on your own understanding, acknowledge him in all your ways, and he will make your paths straight.
Prov 3:5-6.caution: “He will make your paths straight” is not a guarantee of clear answers, but a promise that God leads those who trust him.

Jas 1:5.ctx: James encourages believers going through trials (vv. 2–4) to ask God when they lack wisdom.
Jas 1:5.meaning: God gives generously to all without reproach; anyone who lacks wisdom can ask him with confidence.

Ps 32:8.ctx: David’s psalm of repentance and forgiveness; this verse is God’s answer to the one who repents.
Ps 32:8.meaning: God promises to instruct, to show the way to go, and to counsel with his eye on us.

Ps 27:13-14.ctx: David’s closing declaration while false witnesses rise up and enemies surround him (v. 12).
Ps 27:13-14.meaning: Believing he will see the Lord’s goodness in the land of the living, he says: be strong, let your heart take courage, and wait for the Lord.
Ps 27:13-14.caution: Waiting is not passive giving up; it is continued trust.

Lam 3:25-26.ctx: A lament after the destruction of Jerusalem; in the middle of pain, the writer turns to remembering God’s loving kindness (vv. 21–24).
Lam 3:25-26.meaning: The Lord is good to those who wait for him and seek him; it is good to hope and wait quietly for the Lord’s salvation.

Ps 40:1-3.ctx: David looks back on how God answered his cry; later in the psalm he asks for help again in a new trouble (vv. 11–17).
Ps 40:1-3.meaning: Wait patiently for the Lord and he will hear, lift us out of the pit, and set our feet on a rock.
Ps 40:1-3.caution: The psalmist’s wait may have been long; the text doesn’t say waiting always ends quickly.

Rom 8:26-28.ctx: Paul speaks of creation and believers groaning as they wait for redemption (vv. 18–25).
Rom 8:26-28.meaning: When we are weak and don’t know how to pray, the Spirit himself intercedes for us; all things work together for good for those who love God.
Rom 8:26-28.caution: “All things work together” does not mean every bad thing is good in itself, and it is not a fitting comfort to offer someone who has just been hurt; the point is that God is still in control.

2Cor 4:8-9.ctx: Paul describes the apostles’ suffering in ministry, saying they are like clay jars holding treasure (v. 7).
2Cor 4:8-9.meaning: Pressed on every side but not crushed, perplexed but not in despair, struck down but not destroyed.

Ps 46:1-3.ctx: A psalm of the sons of Korah describing how, amid natural disasters and turmoil among the nations, God is still the refuge of his people.
Ps 46:1-3.meaning: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble; so even if the earth changes, we will not be afraid.

Mark 9:23-24.ctx: A father brings his son, who has a spirit, to Jesus, but the disciples could not heal him (vv. 14–22).
Mark 9:23-24.meaning: The father honestly says, “I believe. Help my unbelief!” and Jesus still responds to him.
Mark 9:23-24.caution: This passage does not say healing depends on having enough faith; the point is that Jesus welcomes imperfect faith.

Ps 13:1-6.ctx: In a long season of trouble, David cries out to God with a lament: “How long?”
Ps 13:1-6.meaning: We can honestly tell God we feel forgotten, and at the same time choose to trust in his loving kindness.

Heb 4:14-16.ctx: The writer of Hebrews encourages persecuted believers who are tempted to turn back to hold fast to their faith.
Heb 4:14-16.meaning: Jesus is a high priest who sympathizes with our weakness, so we can come with boldness to the throne of grace.

Ps 42:5.ctx: A lament of the sons of Korah, written far from the temple while people mocked, “Where is your God?” (v. 3).
Ps 42:5.meaning: The psalmist speaks to his own soul: why are you downcast? Hope in God.
Ps 42:5.caution: This psalm admits that being downcast can return again and again; if a low mood lasts a long time, seeking medical care and counseling is also part of God’s care.

Rom 15:13.ctx: A blessing Paul writes after urging believers of different backgrounds in the Roman church to accept one another (vv. 7–12).
Rom 15:13.meaning: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you abound in hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.

Ps 139:7-12.ctx: A psalm in which David meditates on God’s knowledge and presence everywhere.
Ps 139:7-12.meaning: Wherever we go, God is there; even darkness cannot hide us from him.

Ps 139:13-14.ctx: In the same psalm, David marvels that God formed him in his mother’s womb.
Ps 139:13-14.meaning: We are fearfully and wonderfully made by God’s own hands.

Eph 2:10.ctx: Paul has just explained that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works (vv. 8–9).
Eph 2:10.meaning: We are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for the good works God prepared for us to walk in.

Matt 10:29-31.ctx: Jesus sends out his disciples and warns them that they will face persecution, but tells them not to be afraid (vv. 16–28).
Matt 10:29-31.meaning: God watches over even two sparrows, and the very hairs of our heads are counted; we are worth more than many sparrows.

Prov 16:3.ctx: One of Solomon’s wise sayings about human plans and God’s sovereignty (vv. 1–9).
Prov 16:3.meaning: Commit your works to the Lord, and your plans will succeed.
Prov 16:3.caution: Proverbs are principles of wisdom, not a guarantee that an exam or plan will succeed the way we hope.

Ps 90:17.ctx: A prayer of Moses meditating on the brevity of human life and the eternity of God (vv. 1–12).
Ps 90:17.meaning: Ask that the favor of the Lord be on us, and that he establish the work of our hands.

1Cor 10:13.ctx: Paul uses the history of Israel’s failures in the wilderness as a warning (vv. 1–12) to remind the Corinthian believers.
1Cor 10:13.meaning: No temptation has taken us except what is common to people; God is faithful and will provide a way of escape so that we can endure it.
1Cor 10:13.caution: This verse is about temptation; it does not say God will never allow suffering beyond what we can carry. If your situation feels unbearable, please seek help.

Jas 4:7-8.ctx: James rebukes the fighting and worldly desires among believers (vv. 1–6) and calls them to return.
Jas 4:7-8.meaning: Submit to God and resist the devil; draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.

Ps 37:5-7.ctx: David urges people not to fret because of evildoers, but to trust in the Lord and do good (vv. 1–4).
Ps 37:5-7.meaning: Commit your way to the Lord and wait quietly before him; don’t fret because of those who prosper in their wicked ways.

1Pet 2:21-23.ctx: Peter writes to believers suffering unjust treatment, including those who were servants at the time (vv. 18–20).
1Pet 2:21-23.meaning: When Christ suffered, he did not insult in return or threaten, but entrusted himself to the God who judges righteously.
1Pet 2:21-23.caution: This does not mean staying in oppressive or dangerous situations; when facing bullying, mistreatment at work, or violence, it is right to seek help and protection.

Rom 12:19-21.ctx: Paul urges the Roman believers to treat others with love, even those who persecute them (vv. 14–18).
Rom 12:19-21.meaning: Don’t take revenge yourself; leave justice to God. Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
Rom 12:19-21.caution: “Don’t seek revenge” does not mean giving up on protecting yourself or on seeking help through proper channels.

John 15:4-5.ctx: Jesus’ farewell teaching to his disciples after the Last Supper.
John 15:4-5.meaning: A branch bears fruit only by remaining on the vine; disciples remain in the Lord, and apart from him can do nothing.

Phil 1:6.ctx: From prison, Paul thanks God for the Philippian church’s partnership in the gospel (vv. 3–5).
Phil 1:6.meaning: The God who began a good work in believers will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.

2Pet 1:5-8.ctx: Peter reminds believers that God has already given them everything pertaining to life and godliness (vv. 3–4).
2Pet 1:5-8.meaning: Make every effort to add to your faith moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love.
2Pet 1:5-8.caution: This is growth that comes from grace, not effort to earn God’s love.

1Cor 15:58.ctx: Paul’s conclusion after explaining the hope of the resurrection (chapter 15).
1Cor 15:58.meaning: Because of the hope of resurrection, our labor in the Lord is not in vain.

Gal 6:9-10.ctx: Paul urges the Galatian believers to sow to the Spirit and bear one another’s burdens (vv. 1–8).
Gal 6:9-10.meaning: Don’t grow weary in doing good, for in due season we will reap; as we have opportunity, do good to all.
Gal 6:9-10.caution: The “harvest” comes in God’s time and may not be a visible result.

1Pet 4:10-11.ctx: Peter urges believers in the last days to love one another earnestly and show hospitality (vv. 7–9).
1Pet 4:10-11.meaning: Each one should serve others with the gift received, as good stewards of God’s many kinds of grace, so that God is glorified.

Phil 2:3-5.ctx: Paul urges the Philippian church to be of one mind, then points to Christ’s example of emptying himself (vv. 6–11).
Phil 2:3-5.meaning: Do nothing out of rivalry or conceit, but in humility count others better than yourselves, and have the mind of Christ Jesus.

Gal 6:4-5.ctx: Paul urges believers who restore someone who has fallen to watch themselves and not think too highly of themselves (vv. 1–3).
Gal 6:4-5.meaning: Each one should test their own work, so their boasting is in themselves and not in comparison with someone else; each will carry their own load.

1Pet 5:5-6.ctx: Peter urges elders to shepherd the flock and younger people to submit to their elders (vv. 1–5).
1Pet 5:5-6.meaning: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble; humble yourselves under God’s mighty hand, and he will exalt you in due time.

Num 6:24-26.ctx: God instructs Aaron and his sons to bless the people of Israel with these words (vv. 22–27).
Num 6:24-26.meaning: May the Lord bless and keep you, make his face shine on you, be gracious to you, lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.
Num 6:24-26.caution: Originally a priestly blessing for Israel, it has long been used by the church as a benediction, expressing God’s desire to bless his people.

Ps 103:1-5.ctx: David calls on his own soul to bless the Lord and counts God’s kindnesses.
Ps 103:1-5.meaning: Don’t forget any of God’s benefits: forgiveness, healing, redemption, being crowned with loving kindness and tender mercies.
Ps 103:1-5.caution: “Who heals all your diseases” praises God as the healer; it does not guarantee that every illness will be cured.

1Thess 5:16-18.ctx: A series of short exhortations Paul gives the Thessalonian church at the end of his letter.
1Thess 5:16-18.meaning: Always rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in everything, for this is God’s will in Christ Jesus for us.
1Thess 5:16-18.caution: “In everything give thanks” means giving thanks in all circumstances, not thanking God for evil things themselves.

John 14:27.ctx: Jesus’ farewell words to his disciples on the night he was betrayed, along with his promise that the Holy Spirit would come (vv. 25–26).
John 14:27.meaning: The peace Jesus leaves is not like what the world gives; so don’t let your heart be troubled or afraid.

Isa 26:3-4.ctx: A song to be sung in the land of Judah “in that day,” praising God as a sure stronghold.
Isa 26:3-4.meaning: God keeps in perfect peace those whose minds are steadfast in trusting him, for the Lord is an everlasting Rock.

Ps 4:8.ctx: David’s evening prayer while being disgraced, with many asking, “Who will show us any good?” (vv. 2, 6).
Ps 4:8.meaning: Because the Lord alone makes us live in safety, we can lie down and sleep in peace.

John 3:16-17.ctx: Jesus talks about being “born again” with Nicodemus, a Pharisee who came to him at night (vv. 1–15).
John 3:16-17.meaning: God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that whoever believes in him should have eternal life; God sent him to save, not to condemn.

Eph 2:8-10.ctx: Paul explains that people were dead in trespasses and sins (vv. 1–3), but were made alive through God’s rich mercy.
Eph 2:8-10.meaning: Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works; those who are saved go on to walk in the good works God has prepared.

2Cor 5:17.ctx: Paul speaks of how Christ’s love compels him, because Christ died for all (vv. 14–15).
2Cor 5:17.meaning: If anyone is in Christ, they are a new creation; the old things have passed away, and all things have become new.

Ps 23:4-6.ctx: A psalm of trust David wrote from his experience as a shepherd, moving from green pastures to the valley of the shadow of death, and then to God’s table and house.
Ps 23:4-6.meaning: Even walking through the valley of the shadow of death, there is no need to fear, because God is present; goodness and loving kindness will follow all our days, and we will dwell in the Lord’s house forever.

John 14:1-3.ctx: At the Last Supper, Jesus foretells that he is leaving, and the disciples are troubled (13:33–36).
John 14:1-3.meaning: Jesus goes to prepare a place for his disciples, and he will come again to take them to himself.

Rom 8:38-39.ctx: The conclusion of Paul’s teaching on the hope we have in Christ (chapter 8).
Rom 8:38-39.meaning: Neither death nor life can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.

Ps 34:17-18.ctx: A psalm of thanksgiving David wrote after pretending to be insane before Abimelech (Achish king of Gath) and escaping (see the title).
Ps 34:17-18.meaning: When the righteous cry out, the Lord hears and delivers them from all their troubles; the Lord is near to the brokenhearted.
Ps 34:17-18.caution: “Delivers them” may not mean immediately; please also seek practical protection and help from people around you.

Ps 9:9-10.ctx: David praises God for judging righteously and for not forgetting the cry of the afflicted (v. 12).
Ps 9:9-10.meaning: The Lord is a high tower for the oppressed, a high tower in times of trouble; he has never forsaken those who seek him.

Ps 62:5-8.ctx: A psalm of trust David wrote while surrounded by attackers who bless with their mouths but curse in their hearts (vv. 3–4).
Ps 62:5-8.meaning: Wait in silence for God alone; he is our rock, salvation, and high tower; pour out your heart before him.

Prov 4:23.ctx: Proverbs 4 is a father urging his son to hold on to wisdom; before this he tells him to keep these words in his heart (vv. 20–22), and after it he speaks of the mouth, eyes, and feet (vv. 24–27).
Prov 4:23.meaning: In the Bible the “heart” is the center of thought, emotion, and will; the direction of life flows from it, so guard it with God’s word.
Prov 4:23.caution: This verse is a principle for all of life, not specifically about romance; applied to relationships, it reminds us to care for our own heart first, not to shut ourselves off.

Song 2:7.ctx: Song of Songs is poetry about the love between a bride and groom; this charge appears three times in the book (2:7, 3:5, 8:4), each time after a passage describing the sweetness of love.
Song 2:7.meaning: The bride urges her companions not to stir up or rush love, but to wait for it to mature naturally at the right time.
Song 2:7.caution: This is a charge within a poem; the point is not to rush or force love, not a promise that a particular person will appear at a particular time.

Ps 84:11-12.ctx: Psalm 84 is a pilgrim’s song of longing for God’s house; just before this the psalmist says a day in God’s courts is better than a thousand elsewhere (v. 10).
Ps 84:11-12.meaning: God is a sun (light and provision) and a shield (protection); he gives good things to those who walk blamelessly, and those who trust him are blessed.
Ps 84:11-12.caution: “Good things” are good in God’s eyes; this is not a guarantee of a particular partner or timeline of our choosing.

Deut 6:5-7.ctx: Moses restates the law before Israel enters Canaan; verse 4 is the declaration “Hear, Israel,” and afterward he tells them to bind God’s words on their hands and write them on their doorposts (vv. 8–9).
Deut 6:5-7.meaning: Parents first love God with all their heart and keep his words in their hearts, then diligently teach their children in every moment of life; faith is passed on in everyday life.
Deut 6:5-7.caution: This doesn’t mean parents should lecture constantly, but that faith becomes a natural part of everyday conversation at home.

Eph 6:4.ctx: In Ephesians 5–6 Paul addresses household relationships: he first urges children to obey and honor their parents (6:1–3), then speaks to fathers.
Eph 6:4.meaning: In an era when fathers held great power, Paul tells fathers not to provoke their children through harsh or unfair treatment, but to raise them in the Lord’s discipline and instruction.
Eph 6:4.caution: This verse doesn’t tell parents not to discipline; it says discipline should reflect the Lord’s heart, without anger or shame.

Isa 40:11.ctx: Isaiah 40 begins proclaiming comfort to the exiled people (vv. 1–2); the previous verse says the Lord God will come as a mighty one (v. 10).
Isa 40:11.meaning: The mighty God is also a gentle shepherd: he carries the lambs and gently leads those who have young; he cares for those being cared for, and for those who care for them.
Isa 40:11.caution: This was originally a promise to the people returning from exile; what we can apply is God’s character as a shepherd.

Luke 15:20.ctx: Jesus told three parables to the Pharisees and scribes who criticized him for welcoming sinners (15:1–3); this is the third: after wasting his inheritance, the younger son decides to go home (vv. 11–19).
Luke 15:20.meaning: The father sees him from far away, is moved with compassion, and runs to embrace him, a picture of the heavenly Father’s welcome for those who return, and of a love that does not hold the past against them.
Luke 15:20.caution: The parable is mainly about God’s acceptance of sinners; applied to family, it means learning the father’s heart, not ignoring harm or safe boundaries.

Rom 12:17-18.ctx: In Romans 12 Paul describes life in Christ: weeping with those who weep and being of the same mind toward one another (vv. 15–16), then how to respond to being mistreated (vv. 17–21).
Rom 12:17-18.meaning: Believers don’t repay evil for evil, but pursue peace as far as it depends on them; “if it is possible” also admits that peace depends on both sides.
Rom 12:17-18.caution: Peace does not mean enduring harm; if there is violence or threat, protect your own safety first and seek help from someone you trust.

Gen 50:19-21.ctx: After Jacob dies, Joseph’s brothers fear he will take revenge for their selling him into Egypt, so they send word asking for forgiveness and bow down before him (vv. 15–18).
Gen 50:19-21.meaning: Joseph does not deny his brothers’ evil intent, but sees that God was in control and turned evil into good to save lives; he chooses to forgive and comforts his family with actions and kind words.
Gen 50:19-21.caution: Joseph’s reconciliation with his brothers took years and many tests (Genesis 42–45); healing family relationships also takes time, so don’t force yourself to get there in one step.

Ps 147:3-5.ctx: Psalm 147 is a song of praise after the return from exile; just before this it says the Lord builds up Jerusalem and gathers the outcasts (v. 2).
Ps 147:3-5.meaning: The psalmist places God’s tenderness in healing the brokenhearted beside his greatness in counting the stars: the God who rules the stars also binds up broken hearts himself.

Isa 54:10.ctx: Isaiah 54 compares exiled Israel to a wife forsaken and grieved in spirit (v. 6); God promises to have mercy on her with everlasting kindness and recalls his oath after Noah’s flood (v. 9).
Isa 54:10.meaning: Even if the most solid mountains are moved, God’s loving kindness and covenant of peace will not change.
Isa 54:10.caution: This was originally God’s promise to Israel; what we can apply is God’s unchanging love, not a promise that a lost relationship will come back.

Ps 30:11-12.ctx: Psalm 30 is David’s song of thanksgiving at the dedication of the house, recalling how God lifted him out of the depths; earlier it says “Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning” (v. 5).
Ps 30:11-12.meaning: David testifies that God changed his situation: removing his sackcloth of mourning and clothing him with gladness, so that he would praise God without ceasing.
Ps 30:11-12.caution: This is a testimony looking back after the hard time, not a demand to cheer up right away; grief takes time, and God will walk with you through it.

Ps 121:3-5.ctx: Psalm 121 is a Song of Ascents, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem; it begins by asking, “Where does my help come from?” (vv. 1–2).
Ps 121:3-5.meaning: The God who keeps his people never slumbers, watching over them day and night; we can sleep, because the job of keeping watch belongs to God.
Ps 121:3-5.caution: Ongoing sleeplessness may be connected to physical or emotional health; please also take care of your routine and see a doctor when needed. Trusting God and seeing a doctor do not conflict.

Ps 63:5-8.ctx: According to its title, David wrote Psalm 63 in the wilderness of Judah, longing for God in a dry and weary land (v. 1).
Ps 63:5-8.meaning: Awake at night, David was not swallowed by unease, but remembered how God had helped him, resting like a chick under its mother’s wings.

Ps 3:3-5.ctx: The title of Psalm 3 says David wrote it while fleeing from his son Absalom, when many were rising up against him (vv. 1–2).
Ps 3:3-5.meaning: In a dangerous and distressing situation, after crying out to God, David could still lie down, sleep, and wake up, because God was a shield around him.
